headline: Highest risk is prompt-injection via OpenMetadata’s MCP/API surfaces into plano’s chat-completions workflow; other risks are moderate due to shared data handling and overlapping writes.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenMetadata exposes MCP, APIs, events, and webhooks, so it can emit content that plano may ingest through its OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint. The pair lacks documented provenance tracking or isolation, but direct hijack is not proven. Uncertainty pushes this above low because the interaction pathway is plausible in default integrations.
conditions: IF plano consumes OpenMetadata webhook or MCP payloads as instructions without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF OpenMetadata content is forwarded into plano prompts verbatim, attacker-controlled text can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to every OpenMetadata payload before forwarding.
Strip instruction-like text from webhook/MCP inputs.
Require an allowlist of fields passed from OpenMetadata to plano.
Insert a human review step for any prompt assembled from catalog content.
requires-engineering: add schema validation and signed-message verification between systems.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenMetadata touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal knowledge, while plano handles logs, traces, and metrics and has broad network egress. If they share a workspace or exchange files, sensitive operational metadata can flow into plano and then out to third parties. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this remains inferred but credible.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata exports governance or lineage artifacts into a shared workspace, plano can ingest them.
IF plano forwards those artifacts through its broad network egress, leakage to external services can occur.
mitigations: Keep OpenMetadata and plano on separate workspaces.
Disable forwarding of logs/traces containing catalog content.
Redact governance and lineage fields before any handoff.
Review outbound destinations in plano’s config.yaml.
requires-engineering: enforce per-field data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenMetadata supports multiple instances and can write via APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP; plano has broad network egress and no multiple-instance support. Their write surfaces can overlap on shared mutable resources, creating race conditions or conflicting updates. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same downstream API or dataset without locks, updates can conflict.
IF plano relays OpenMetadata changes while OpenMetadata also writes directly, last-write-wins corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign one agent as the sole writer for each resource.
Use optimistic concurrency tokens on shared records.
Serialize writes through a queue or lock service.
Separate read-only and write-only credentials.
requires-engineering: add transactional conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata can produce catalog, lineage, and governance outputs that plano may treat as input to routing or downstream actions. Plano’s chat-completions gateway role suggests it may pass along those outputs without independent verification. Because the exact orchestration is undocumented, the interaction is inferred, but the default pathway is plausible enough for medium.
conditions: IF plano uses OpenMetadata-generated metadata as authoritative routing context, errors can cascade.
IF OpenMetadata emits stale lineage or governance facts and plano forwards them unchanged, downstream decisions can be wrong.
mitigations: Require plano to verify critical fields against source systems.
Mark OpenMetadata-derived fields as advisory, not authoritative.
Add freshness checks before forwarding metadata.
Log and review mismatches between source and forwarded values.
requires-engineering: implement cross-system validation rules.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenMetadata explicitly touches governance and memory/tribal knowledge, while plano handles logs and traces; that creates a compliance surface, but no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. Because the profiles do not show a concrete regulatory conflict, this is a low-severity gap rather than a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in OpenMetadata and mirrored into plano logs, retention policy mismatch becomes relevant.
IF either deployment is placed under a residency or certification requirement not shown in the profiles, compliance review is needed.
mitigations: Inventory which regulated data classes each system stores.
Set log retention to the minimum needed.
Exclude secrets from plano logs.
Document residency and certification assumptions.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across both systems.
